title: System Design How to store passwords in the database

segments.text: How do we store passwords safely in the database?
How do we validate a password or user enter against what we store in the database?
Let's take a look.
It is essential to store passwords in a way that keeps an attacker from getting them, even if the database is compromised.
Let's talk about what not to do first.
Do not store passwords in plain text.
Anyone with internal access to the database can see them.
If the database is compromised, an attacker could easily get all the passwords.
So what should we do to save restore password in the database?
The open web application security project, also known as OWSP,
provided some guidelines on how to store passwords.
Here are the recommendations.
First, use a modern hashing algorithm.
Hashing is a one way function.
It is impossible to decrip a hash to obtain the original value.
If an attacker obtains the hashed password,
they can not just enter it into the application to gain access.
It is important to use a modern hashing function designed for to securely store passwords.
These are sometimes characterized as slow functions that use more resources to compute.
This makes brute-for-actex and attractive.
Note that some common legacy hashing function like MD5 and SHA1 are fast.
There are less secure and should not be used.
Second, salt the passwords.
According to the OWSP guidelines, a salt is a unique randomly generated strain
that is added to each password as a part of the hashing process.
Why do we need to salt the password at all?
So storing a password as a one way hash is a step in the right direction,
but it is not sufficient.
An attacker can defeat one way hashes with pre-computation attacks.
Some common attacks are rainbow tables and database-based lookups.
With these techniques, a hacker could crack a password in seconds.
By adding a salt that is unique to each password to the hashing process,
it ensures that the hashes unique to each password.
This simple technique makes pre-computation attacks unattractive.
Let's take a look at how we store a password and is salt.
We first combine the password provided by the user with the randomly generated salt.
We then compute the hash of this combination using an appropriate hashing function.
The hash is stored in the database along with the salt.
Again, the salt is used to generate a unique hash.
It is not a secret and can be stored safely as plain attacks in the database.
Finally, let's take a look at the process in reverse.
When the user locks in, how do we validate the password against what is stored in the database?
First, we fetch the salt for the user from the database.
We then append the salt to the password provided by the user and hash it.
We compare this computer hash against the hash stored in the database.
If they are the same, the password is valid.
That's it about storing passwords in the database.

Please subscribe if you learned something new.
Thank you so much and we'll see you next time.
